caption.text:
🚨 Flaky Playwright tests? Don't just add retries!

A retry can hide a flaky test—but it doesn't fix the root cause.
In this reel, I explain 7 practical steps to handle flaky tests in Playwright:
🔹 Identify the root cause
🔹 Use auto-waiting & web-first assertions
🔹 Choose reliable locators
🔹 Handle async operations properly
🔹 Keep tests independent
🔹 Use retries as a safety net
🔹 Debug using Trace Viewer, screenshots & reports

💡 Interview Tip:
Don't simply say “I use retries.”
A stronger answer is:
Root Cause → Stabilize → Retry → Monitor

That shows you're actually solving the problem instead of hiding flaky failures.

caption.text:
Your Playwright tests pass today... but fail tomorrow? 🤔

That's called a flaky test, and it's one of the biggest challenges in test automation.

In this reel, I share 5 practical ways to reduce flaky tests:

✔️ Use stable locators like getByRole() and getByTestId()
✔️ Avoid waitForTimeout()
✔️ Wait for real application conditions
✔️ Keep every test independent
✔️ Use Playwright's auto-retrying assertions

One important point to remember:

👉 Retries can help detect flaky tests, but they should never be used to hide the real problem. Always investigate and fix the root cause.

These are the same practices used in production automation frameworks to build stable and reliable test suites.

🟢 Flaky Playwright tests? The problem may not be your selector - it could be the wrong timeout. ⏱️

🟢 Flaky Playwright tests may be caused by the wrong timeout—not just a bad selector.

🟢 Test timeout - 30 seconds by default for the complete test flow.

🟢 Expect timeout - 5 seconds for retrying web-first assertions.

🟢 Action timeout - 0 by default for actions such as `click()`, `fill()`, and `check()`.

🟢 Navigation timeout - 0 by default for `goto()`, `reload()`, and other navigation operations.

🟢 Web-server timeout - 60 seconds for the configured application server to start.

🟢 Global timeout - Disabled by default; when configured, it limits the entire test run.

🟢 Fixtures and hooks - Consume timeout budgets, while slow fixtures can have dedicated limits.

🟢 `test.slow()` - Triples the applicable test timeout.

🟢 Auto-waiting - Waits for elements to become visible, stable, enabled, and ready for interaction.

🟢 Web-first assertions - Automatically retry until the expected condition passes or the timeout expires.

🟢 Fixed waits - Avoid `page.waitForTimeout(5000)` because it makes tests slower and less reliable.

🟢 Smart waiting - Wait for real signals such as visibility, enabled state, URL changes, responses, or application state.

🟢 Locator timeout - A locator has no universal standalone timeout; the action, assertion, navigation, or explicit wait owns it.

🟢 Troubleshooting - Identify which timeout expired before increasing any value.

🟢 Best practice - Increase only the timeout that genuinely needs more time.

🟢 Save this post for your next flaky-test investigation! 🚀

caption.text:
🔵 How do you find a hole you can’t see?
A microscopic crack, a tiny channel, or an almost invisible seal defect can be enough to compromise the integrity of pharmaceutical packaging.
So, how can you detect something you can’t see?
A Dye Immersion Leak Test combines three simple elements:
🔹 A colored liquid
🔹 Vacuum
🔹 Visual inspection
The package is immersed in dye, vacuum is applied, and when the vacuum is released, the pressure difference can draw the dye through a leak path—turning an invisible defect into visible evidence.
🎥 In Episode 1 of our Dye Immersion Leak Test Series, we explain the basic principle behind methylene blue leak testing and why vacuum plays such an important role in revealing package defects.
This is the first episode of a 9-part educational series dedicated to Dye Immersion Leak Testing for pharmaceutical packaging.
📩 Need to improve, validate, or standardize your pharmaceutical leak testing process?
Our technical team can help you evaluate your packaging, test method, vacuum parameters, and equipment requirements.
